titre: Gideon v. Wainwright: The Lawyer a Pencil Petition Won
accroche: In 1962, a prisoner wrote in pencil, on prison-issued lined paper, to demand the lawyer he had been denied. The Supreme Court sided with him in 1963, unanimously.
contenu_vulgarise:
On January 5, 1962, Clarence Earl Gideon wrote, in pencil, on lined paper supplied by the Florida prison where he was held, a petition addressed to the Supreme Court of the United States. He described himself as indigent and claimed he had been unconstitutionally denied the right to a lawyer at his trial for breaking into a pool hall. He had been sentenced to five years in prison after conducting his own defense: Florida law provided a court-appointed lawyer only in capital cases.

## A right that stopped at the states' door

The Sixth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution guarantees, in any criminal prosecution, the accused's right to the assistance of counsel. For federal courts, the Supreme Court had already ruled that this right applied to people without means, absent a valid waiver. But in 1942, in Betts v. Brady, the Court had refused to extend that obligation to state courts, holding that the lack of a lawyer did not, by itself, make a trial unfair. Twenty years later, it was this very precedent that Gideon's petition, written from his cell, set out to challenge.

The Court agreed to hear the case and appointed Abe Fortas, a prominent Washington lawyer who would himself later become a Supreme Court justice, to represent Gideon. The case was argued on January 15, 1963. On March 18, the Supreme Court ruled unanimously, nine votes to zero: Betts v. Brady had to be overruled. The opinion, written by Justice Hugo Black, borrowed the very words of the 1942 ruling to reverse its conclusion: the right to counsel is "fundamental and essential to a fair trial." From then on, protected by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, that right bound the states too, not only federal courts.

## What a sheet of lined paper changes

Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335 (1963), was made possible by a document no one but its author had reason to take seriously: a handwritten petition, drafted without legal training, by a man who had neither the means nor, until then, the right to be represented. The Supreme Court treated it as a petition for review (a writ of certiorari) worthy of the same consideration as a brief drafted by a law firm. Gideon was granted a second trial, this time with a court-appointed lawyer. He was acquitted.

The original petition, kept at the National Archives and now on display in Washington, settles nothing by itself: a handwritten document on prison paper carries no legal authority of its own. What changed American law was not the petition; it was the Court's decision to read it through rather than file it away. Between the hand that wrote in pencil and the hand that signed the ruling, there is no necessary link, only nine justices who chose not to stop at the document's form before examining its substance.

citation.texte: Upon full reconsideration we conclude that Betts v. Brady should be overruled.
citation.auteur: Justice Hugo Black, opinion of the Court

carte.punch: In 1962, a prisoner wrote in pencil to demand the lawyer he had been denied.
carte.idee: Clarence Earl Gideon wrote, in 1962, from his cell, a handwritten petition to the Supreme Court. In 1963 the Court ruled unanimously that states must provide a lawyer to indigent defendants, overturning twenty years of contrary precedent. Retried with a lawyer, Gideon was acquitted.

quiz.question: What does the U.S. Supreme Court rule in Gideon v. Wainwright (1963)?
choix: The right to a lawyer for indigent defendants also binds state courts, not only federal courts
Only capital offenses entitle a defendant to a court-appointed lawyer in every state
Handwritten petitions can no longer be considered by the Supreme Court
Betts v. Brady (1942) remains in force, but only in Florida
quiz.explication: The Court rules unanimously that the right to counsel, guaranteed by the Sixth Amendment, is protected against the states by the Fourteenth Amendment, and overturns Betts v. Brady (1942). Florida's law, which limited court-appointed counsel to capital cases, is exactly what the ruling strikes down; handwritten petitions remain admissible, since one of them is how the case began.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What had the Supreme Court decided in Betts v. Brady (1942), which Gideon v. Wainwright overturns twenty years later?
choix: The lack of a lawyer in a state trial does not, by itself, make that trial unfair
No defendant, even in federal court, has a right to a court-appointed lawyer
Only lawyers admitted by the Supreme Court may argue criminal cases
States cannot try any criminal case without a federal judge's approval
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Betts v. Brady (1942) held that the lack of a lawyer did not, by itself, make a state trial unfair, leaving states free not to provide one outside capital cases. The ruling did not deny the right to counsel in federal courts, did not reserve pleading to lawyers admitted by the Supreme Court, and did not subject state trials to a federal judge's approval.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Whom does the Supreme Court appoint to defend Clarence Earl Gideon before it?
choix: Abe Fortas, a Washington lawyer who would himself later become a Supreme Court justice
Hugo Black, the justice who would go on to write the Court's opinion
A Florida lawyer, appointed by the state that was prosecuting Gideon
No lawyer: Gideon kept conducting his own defense before the Court
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Court appoints Abe Fortas, a prominent Washington lawyer, who becomes a Supreme Court justice a few years later. Hugo Black is the justice who writes the Court's opinion, not Gideon's lawyer; the State of Florida is the opposing party, and Gideon is indeed represented before the Supreme Court, unlike at his first trial.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens to Clarence Earl Gideon after the Supreme Court's ruling?
choix: He is retried with a court-appointed lawyer, and is acquitted
His original conviction is permanently voided, with no new trial
He stays in prison: the ruling applies only to future cases
He is retried but convicted a second time, to a harsher sentence
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Gideon is granted a second trial, this time with a court-appointed lawyer, and is acquitted. The Supreme Court does not itself issue a final acquittal with no new trial, the ruling applies to his own case and not only to future ones, and he is not convicted a second time.
